skills.description: Use when writing, reviewing, debugging, or refactoring Swift or SwiftUI code for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or watchOS apps and packages.
skills.content:
---
name: Swift and SwiftUI engineering
description: >-
  Use when writing, reviewing, debugging, or refactoring Swift or SwiftUI code
  for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or watchOS apps and packages.
---
# Swift and SwiftUI engineering

## Defaults
- Target the deployment OS the project already sets; check `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` or `Package.swift` before using a newer API, and guard newer APIs with `if #available`.
- Swift concurrency first: `async`/`await`, structured tasks, `@MainActor` on UI-facing types. Turn on strict concurrency checking for new code and fix warnings rather than silencing them.
- SwiftUI state: `@State` for view-local values, `@Observable` models (iOS 17+) or `ObservableObject` for older targets, `@Environment` for shared dependencies. One source of truth per value.
- Value types (`struct`, `enum`) by default; `final class` only when identity or reference semantics are needed.
- Swift Package Manager for dependencies unless the project already standardized on something else. Never invent package names or versions; check the package's real repo.
- Secrets never go in source, `Info.plist`, or the asset catalog. Use the Keychain on device and a server for anything truly secret.

## Practice
1. Read the existing project structure, scheme, and targets before adding files; match its naming and folder layout.
2. Keep views small. Extract subviews and move logic into models or services so it can be unit tested without UI.
3. Networking: `URLSession` with `async` APIs, `Codable` models, explicit error types, and timeouts. Never block the main thread.
4. Persistence: SwiftData (iOS 17+) or Core Data for structured data, `UserDefaults` only for small preferences, Keychain for credentials.
5. Accessibility from the start: Dynamic Type, VoiceOver labels on icon-only controls, sufficient contrast, hit targets of at least 44 by 44 points.
6. Add or update `#Preview` blocks so each screen renders with sample data.
7. Test with Swift Testing (`@Test`, `#expect`) or XCTest, whichever the project uses. Run them with `xcodebuild test -scheme <Scheme> -destination '<simulator>'` and read failures before claiming done.
8. Build from the command line to confirm: `xcodebuild -scheme <Scheme> -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' build`. A change isn't done until it compiles without new warnings.
9. When a platform behavior is uncertain, check Apple's current documentation at developer.apple.com rather than relying on memory; APIs change every year.

## Anti-jobs
- No force unwraps (`!`) or `try!` on data from the network, disk, or the user.
- No `DispatchQueue.main.async` sprinkled to hide concurrency warnings.
- No retain cycles: use `[weak self]` in escaping closures that capture `self` on classes.
- No private or undocumented APIs; they get apps rejected.
- No committing signing certificates, provisioning profiles, `.p8` keys, or API keys.

skills.name: App Store review readiness
skills.description: Use before submitting an iOS or macOS app (or an update) to App Store review, or when diagnosing an App Review rejection.
skills.content:
---
name: App Store review readiness
description: >-
  Use before submitting an iOS or macOS app (or an update) to App Store review,
  or when diagnosing an App Review rejection.
---
# App Store review readiness

Apple's rules change. Before relying on any item below, check the live [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) and quote the current section number in your findings.

## Never without the owner's yes
- Never press Submit for Review, release a build, change pricing, or accept agreements. Prepare the checklist and the metadata, then hand it to the account owner.

## Pre-submission checklist
1. **Completeness (2.1).** No placeholder text, broken links, crashes, or dead buttons. Test on a real device and on the smallest and largest supported screens.
2. **Reviewer access.** If the app needs a login, supply a working demo account and any steps in App Review Information notes. If features depend on hardware or a server, say how to reach them.
3. **Accurate metadata (2.3).** Screenshots show the real app on the right device sizes; the description, keywords, and age rating match what the app does.
4. **Privacy (5.1).**
   - A privacy policy URL that loads.
   - App Privacy details (the nutrition label) in App Store Connect that match what the app and every SDK actually collect.
   - A privacy manifest (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`) declaring required-reason APIs, and third-party SDKs carrying their own manifests and signatures.
   - Purpose strings (`NSCameraUsageDescription`, `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`, `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription`, location, photos, and so on) for every permission requested, written in plain words.
   - Ask for permissions in context, not all at launch.
5. **Account deletion (5.1.1(v)).** If users can create an account in the app, they must be able to start deleting it in the app.
6. **Sign in with Apple (4.8).** Check the current rule if the app offers third-party or social login.
7. **Payments (3.1).** Digital goods and subscriptions use In-App Purchase unless a current exception applies. Subscriptions show price, period, and terms before purchase, include Restore Purchases, and link the terms of use and privacy policy.
8. **Minimum functionality (4.2) and spam (4.3).** The app must do more than wrap a website, and must not duplicate an existing app of the same developer.
9. **User-generated content (1.2).** Needs reporting, blocking, and a way to filter objectionable material.
10. **AI and generated content.** Check the current guidelines on generated content, content moderation, and disclosure of sharing data with third-party AI.
11. **Export compliance.** Set `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` in `Info.plist` correctly so each build doesn't stall on the encryption question.
12. **Build hygiene.** Built with the currently required Xcode and SDK version (check Apple's upcoming-requirements page), no private APIs, no debug menus or test endpoints reachable in release.

## Handling a rejection
1. Read the full message in Resolution Center and note the guideline numbers cited.
2. Open those exact sections on the live guidelines page.
3. Decide whether to fix the build, fix metadata only, or reply with a clarification. Draft the reply for the owner; don't send it yourself.
4. If the rejection seems mistaken, the owner can appeal through the App Review Board.

## Report back
A pass, fix, or unknown line for each checklist item, with the guideline section and the evidence (file, screen, or setting) for each.

skills.name: TestFlight and code signing
skills.description: Use when signing, archiving, uploading, or distributing an iOS build through TestFlight or direct device install, or when fixing provisioning and certificate errors.
skills.content:
---
name: TestFlight and code signing
description: >-
  Use when signing, archiving, uploading, or distributing an iOS build through
  TestFlight or direct device install, or when fixing provisioning and
  certificate errors.
---
# TestFlight and code signing

Check Apple's current [TestFlight overview](https://developer.apple.com/testflight/) and Xcode documentation before quoting limits or steps; they change.

## Never without the owner's yes
- No external TestFlight groups or public links (those require Beta App Review and reach people outside the team).
- No new paid Developer Program enrollment, no revoking certificates, no deleting App IDs or profiles.
- Never paste or commit `.p12`, `.p8`, `.mobileprovision`, or App Store Connect API keys. Keep them in the Keychain or a secret store.

## Prerequisites
1. Full Xcode installed (not just Command Line Tools): `xcode-select -p` should point inside `Xcode.app`, and `xcodebuild -version` should run.
2. An Apple Developer team. A free personal team can install to the owner's own devices for 7 days per build; TestFlight and the App Store need the paid program.
3. A unique bundle identifier registered under that team.

## Signing
1. Prefer Automatic Signing in Xcode (Signing & Capabilities, choose the team). It creates and renews certificates and profiles.
2. Add capabilities (push, iCloud, App Groups, Sign in with Apple) in Xcode so the App ID and profile update together.
3. For headless or CI builds, use an App Store Connect API key with `xcodebuild -allowProvisioningUpdates -authenticationKeyPath ... -authenticationKeyID ... -authenticationKeyIssuerID ...`, with the key path coming from a secret store.
4. Common errors:
   - "No profiles for ... were found": team not selected, or the bundle ID isn't registered; enable automatic signing or register it.
   - "Device not registered" for development builds: add the device UDID in the developer account or connect it to Xcode once.
   - Expired or missing distribution certificate: let Xcode create a new one; don't revoke the old one without the owner's yes.

## Archive and upload
1. Bump `CFBundleVersion` (build number) for every upload; `CFBundleShortVersionString` is the marketing version.
2. Archive: `xcodebuild -scheme <Scheme> -configuration Release -archivePath build/App.xcarchive archive`.
3. Export with an `ExportOptions.plist` (method `app-store-connect`, team ID, signing style automatic): `xcodebuild -exportArchive -archivePath build/App.xcarchive -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist -exportPath build/export`. Setting `destination` to `upload` in that plist uploads directly.
4. Otherwise upload with Xcode Organizer or the Transporter app, using whichever command-line upload tool Apple currently documents for headless runs. Confirm the build appears in App Store Connect and finishes processing.
5. Answer export compliance, ideally by setting `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` in `Info.plist` ahead of time.

## Distribute
- **Internal testers:** members of the App Store Connect team; builds are available after processing with no review.
- **External testers:** need Beta App Review for the first build of a version, plus test information and a feedback email. Owner's yes required.
- TestFlight builds expire after a fixed period (currently 90 days); upload a fresh build before testers lose access.
- **Direct install without TestFlight:** a development-signed build to a registered device via Xcode or `xcrun devicectl device install app --device <id> <path.app>`.

## Report back
The team, bundle ID, version and build number, where the build is (archived, uploaded, processing, available to internal testers), and any blocker that needs the owner, such as an Apple ID sign-in or 2FA.

skills.name: iOS app builder getting started
skills.description: Use as the first conversation of a newly imported iOS app-building bot with its new owner, to learn their setup before building anything.
skills.content:
---
name: iOS app builder getting started
description: >-
  Use as the first conversation of a newly imported iOS app-building bot with
  its new owner, to learn their setup before building anything.
---
# Getting started

I help you build iOS apps in Swift and SwiftUI, from design through TestFlight. I can also help with iPhone-side setup for the apps we build, like Shortcuts and settings. Nothing gets submitted to the App Store, opened to external testers, or paid for without your yes.

Ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:

1. What should I call you, and is there an app you want to start on (or improve)?
2. Which Mac will do the builds? Does it have full Xcode installed, or only Command Line Tools? If you've registered it as one of your computers, I can run builds there with your approval.
3. Are you in the paid Apple Developer Program, and what's your team name? (Never paste passwords, certificates or API keys into chat.)
4. Which of these do you use or want? I'll show a connect card for each one you pick: Figma (designs to SwiftUI), Mobbin (real app UI references), Firebase (backend), Sentry (crash reports), RevenueCat (subscriptions), Tuist (project generation and build insights), Revyl (run the app on cloud devices). Grok Voice needs no sign-in and can add voice chat, dictation and read-aloud.
5. Where should the code live (GitHub, another host, or a new repo), and are there rules I should follow, such as who approves changes, things never to delete, or naming?

After the answers:
- Save each answer as a memory (name, build Mac, team, code location, rules).
- Offer connect cards only for the services they chose.
- If Xcode is missing, explain what installing it needs before any build work.
- Then start on their first app: confirm the goal in one or two sentences, propose a small first version, and begin once they agree.
